title: "In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful"
hook: the opening — seven verses said seventeen times a day, and the first is a name
carry: in the name of the merciful
tomorrow: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds"

segments.voice: Yesterday: the five pillars. Five things that hold a life up, on clocks from a breath to a lifetime. Which one did you notice holding yours? Day six.
screen: `THE FIVE PILLARS — ALWAYS, DAILY, YEARLY, ONCE.`

segments.voice: Think of the thing you've said most often in your life. Your own name. Hello. Probably I'm fine. Now picture a prayer seven verses long, said seventeen times every day in the required prayers, by a child of seven and a woman of ninety, in a desert, a city apartment, an airport corner. Over a lifetime, that's hundreds of thousands of times. Whatever that prayer says, it's going to wear a groove in a person. It's called al-Fatiha. For the next seven days, we'll walk through it one verse a day. And the first verse is one you already know.
screen: `SEVEN VERSES.` → `SEVENTEEN TIMES A DAY.` → `ONE VERSE A DAY, FOR SEVEN DAYS.`

segments.voice: Al-Fatiha means the opening. It's the first surah of the Qur'an, and its root, f-t-h, is the root of opening things: a door, a way, a city. The Arabic word for a key, miftah, grows from it too. The Qur'an speaks of seven oft-repeated verses, and many scholars read that as al-Fatiha. A hadith in Bukhari says there is no prayer without it. That's where the seventeen comes from: the five daily prayers add up to seventeen units, and every unit begins with these seven verses. Now, verse one. In the numbering Pickthall follows, and most printed copies of the Qur'an today, the first verse is the line you met on day two. In his words: “In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful.” Bismillah ar-rahman ar-rahim. On day two it was the words before a meal or a drive. Here it's the first step into the prayer itself. Listen to the shape of it. The prayer doesn't open with a request, or with the one praying at all. It opens by stepping inside a name, the way you'd walk through a door someone is holding. Everything after this is said in that name. And which name? Not the powerful one, not the judge. The two names chosen for the doorway are both mercy. We'll open those two words properly on day eight. For today, just notice where the most repeated prayer in a Muslim's life begins: in a name, and the name is merciful. Verse one of seven.
screen: `THE OPENING — F-T-H, A KEY.` · `NO PRAYER WITHOUT IT.` · `VERSE ONE: THE DAY-TWO LINE.` · `THROUGH THE DOOR OF A NAME.` · then, large: `IN THE NAME OF THE MERCIFUL.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. Picture a doorway in front of you, and someone kind holding the door. First breath: stand at the threshold. Second breath: step through. Third breath: notice that whatever you do next, you're doing it from inside. If you want, let the line go out with the last breath: bismillah ar-rahman ar-rahim.
Al-Fatiha. The opening: seven verses at the start of the Qur'an, and at the start of every unit of every prayer. Sixth word.
Your line: in the name of the merciful. Today, begin one conversation that could go either way with the gentlest first sentence you have. Day six.

screen: `DAY 6 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: "PRAISE BE TO ALLAH, LORD OF THE WORLDS."`

howItsDone: Muslims recite al-Fatiha in Arabic in every unit of every prayer, and at many other moments: over the sick, at a wedding, for someone who has died. When it ends in prayer, most Sunni Muslims say amin; Shia Muslims of the Ja'fari school do not say amin in the prayer.

match.prompt: what's inside the opening — tap the pairs.
pairs: units in the five daily prayers

myth: al-Fatiha is said once a day
seventeen times a day in the required prayers: it begins every unit of every prayer.
in Pickthall's numbering, the bismillah is verse one of al-Fatiha
most printed copies count it as 1:1; some counts don't number it as a verse.
the root of fatiha also makes the Arabic word for a key
f-t-h, to open: a key is a miftah.

fork.setup: someone new to the prayer knows very little Arabic yet. which part does a hadith in Bukhari say no prayer can be without?
fork.reveal: there is no prayer without al-Fatiha. that's why it's usually among the first things a learner memorizes.

original.note: Arabic: "the opening." from f-t-h, to open, the same root as miftah, a key.

trapdoor: what you thought: the first chapter, like a preface.
what it means: the opening — seven verses said in every unit of every prayer, beginning in a merciful name.

what a scholar hears: the Qur'an's "seven oft-repeated" (15:87) is widely read as al-Fatiha; whether the bismillah is its first verse depends on the verse count, and the schools differ on reciting it aloud.

sources.quoted: In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 756; Sahih Muslim 394 (no prayer without al-Fatiha)

notes: Re-ordered camp one (owner, 2026-09-30): al-Fatiha now runs one verse a day, days 6–12, in Pickthall's (Kufan) numbering with the bismillah as 1:1. Other counts don't number the bismillah as a verse, and the schools differ on reciting it aloud in prayer (and the Maliki school on reciting it in the obligatory prayer at all). A Keeper may want one sentence on this.
'Seventeen times a day': the seventeen required units (2+4+4+3+4); travelers who shorten prayers recite fewer. Confirm.
Hadith numbers Bukhari 756 / Muslim 394 cited from memory; please confirm. The Hanafi school treats reciting al-Fatiha as required (wajib) rather than a pillar; the script only reports the hadith.
howItsDone mentions al-Fatiha recited over the sick, at weddings and for the dead: common practice in many communities, not universal. Confirm the wording.
Amin after al-Fatiha: stated as most Sunni Muslims say it; Ja'fari Shia do not in prayer. Confirm.
